BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The pattern through the extended will consist of a broad upper level ridge extending across the western/central CONUS while a longwave trough persists over the Gulf of Alaska and clips the Pacific Northwest.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to slightly above normal temperatures through Friday.
- Isolated showers north of Baker City to McCall today.
- Above normal temperatures and mostly dry over the weekend into early next week. Stagnant conditions in the lower valleys with temperature inversions possible.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A weak upper level trough will move across the area today. This will bring isolated showers north of Baker City to McCall, with about a 10% chance of showers across the central Idaho mountains this afternoon. A dusting of snow will be possible in the mountains above 4500-6000 feet MSL. Elsewhere, it will be dry with decreasing clouds this afternoon. Highs will be near normal, and winds today will be locally breezy with gusts up to 20 mph south of Boise. An upper level ridge will build across the area Friday and Saturday, bringing dry conditions and warming temperatures. Skies will be mostly cloudy on Friday but mostly clear on Saturday. Warming will be aided by southwest flow aloft that develops in response to a trough approaching the Washington coast on Saturday, with highs reaching around 10 degrees above normal. This system will also result in breezy southeast winds across the area. Patchy fog will develop each night through the end of the week in sheltered basins.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The pattern through the extended will consist of a broad upper level ridge extending across the western/central CONUS while a longwave trough persists over the Gulf of Alaska and clips the Pacific Northwest. This will place our area in southwest flow aloft and keep temperatures 10-15 degrees above normal. A system moving across Washington on Sunday and another weak system on Monday will produce a 10-20% chance of showers across the north with only increased clouds to the south. Additional systems will move to the north through midweek, with precipitation chances gradually rising to 20-30% across the north by Thursday. Winds will be breezy on Sunday and again Wednesday/Thursday as systems pass by to the north. However, light winds Monday and Tuesday and the ridge of high pressure may result in stagnant valley conditions and temperature inversions.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: From Saturday through at least Wednesday, ridging aloft will be firmly in place for our area. Above average temperatures are likely to prevail under mostly sunny skies.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light mountain snow possible on Friday in the high country north of I-70.
- Pleasant temperatures and dry conditions are expected Thursday and then Saturday through early next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Current radar shows the snow for the high country only lingering in the southern third of Park County. Some additional snow of 1-2" will be possible there over the next few hours as the upper- level low shifts off to the east. We expect the Winter Weather Advisory to be allowed to expire at 2 AM Thursday. Some light rain is also ongoing in far southern Lincoln County. A few more scattered rain showers remain possible there, but this chance quickly ends by 5 AM this morning. Lows tonight are forecast to be similar to last night with temperatures near or just above freezing for the plains and in the upper teens to 20s for the high country. Thursday should be a pleasant day as a ridge aloft briefly builds in. We expect mostly sunny skies and high temperatures in the mid to upper 50s for the plains.

The trough on Friday has trended a bit further south since last night, but moisture still looks minimal along with poor lift. Most short-term guidance is showing at least some QPF for the central and northern high country. Thus, Friday afternoon and evening now has the chance for some light mountain snow above 8,500 ft. This forecast remains in line with the previous package. For locations in the high country mainly north of I-70, we are forecasting 2 inches of snow or less with perhaps a few locations approaching 3 inches. REFS DESI probabilities show the chance for any locations in our area to receive >2 inches to be around 30% or less. RMNP, the Mummy Range, the Indian Peaks, and the Never Summer Mountains are most favored for the "higher" totals. Model soundings show these locations could have a small amount of weak upslope. Some light widely scattered rain showers could spread into Weld County along and west of I-25, but there is only a 15% chance or less. Otherwise, expect highs on Friday in the mid to upper 50s for the plains with a slight increase in clouds compared to the last few days.

From Saturday through at least Wednesday, ridging aloft will be firmly in place for our area. Above average temperatures are likely to prevail under mostly sunny skies. Ensemble guidance continues to hone in on Sunday and Monday as the warmest days of the week with high temperatures in the mid to upper 60s for the urban corridor and highs near 70 F on the far eastern plains. High temperatures look to stay in the low to mid 60s from Wednesday onward as the ridge shifts a bit to the south. Any precipitation looks highly unlikely after Friday through at least the end of the forecast period.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Monday-Wednesday...Dry west northwest flow aloft prevails with a few shortwave troughs aloft passing by, though with minimal low and mid level moisture, no precipitation expected. High temperatures nearly the same each day based on 700 mb temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near average temperatures and mostly dry conditions are expected through the remainder of the work week.
- Warmer temperatures are likely to return this weekend with dry weather conditions continuing.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Mid to high-level clouds are currently being fed into the CWA from a trough to our east across the Upper Midwest. These clouds may limit radiational cooling for the overnight hours, so lows tonight may only dip into the low to mid 20s west of I-25 and around 30 east of the corridor. While highs Thursday will jump back into the upper 40s to low 50s from the Laramie Range and west, with temperatures soaring into the mid to upper 50s east of the mountains. Lets switch gears a bit and look at the synoptic features aloft. High pressure located over southeast Montana is forming a Rex Block over our region, this will bring benign weather conditions across the CWA for today. This will clear out the remaining mid to high-level clouds, west to east, through the morning hours as the high pressure shifts east. We will see a return of cloud cover later this afternoon/evening as a weak shortwave begins to push in from the west, breaking down the Rex Block. By Friday, the aforementioned shortwave aloft will slide east across the state, this will increase precipitation chances primarily over the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges, albeit slight. Everywhere else across the CWA is expected to stay dry with additional cloud cover being the only sign that something, such as a weak cold front, is passing through. This additional cloud cover will keep highs slightly cooler than Thursday, but still near normal for early November.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: No major changes in the long term, except for taking out Friday and starting the long term discussion on Saturday, please see previous discussion below...
Saturday...Will see a slow warming trend though tempered by northerly flow aloft. Low and mid levels look too dry for any precipitation.

Sunday...The warming trend continues as the ridge aloft builds across our counties, helping to produce a surface lee trough across eastern Wyoming. 700 mb temperatures near 7 Celsius will yield maximum temperatures from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

Monday-Wednesday...Dry west northwest flow aloft prevails with a few shortwave troughs aloft passing by, though with minimal low and mid level moisture, no precipitation expected. High temperatures nearly the same each day based on 700 mb temperatures.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Snow showers are expected in the central mountains until around sunrise. Travel in these areas may be impacted by snow and icy roads mainly at pass level. Lingering moisture and clearing skies could result in pockets of fog into Thursday morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rivers and other waterways across southeast Utah are still elevated due to runoff. Flood Warnings remain in effect for those impacted areas.

- Valley rain and mountain snow will continue through late tonight and early Thursday morning, respectively. 4 to 8 inches of snow is expected above 10,000 feet across parts of the central Colorado mountains where a Winter Weather Advisory has been issued.
- Warmer and drier conditions highlight the remainder of the seven-day forecast.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Snow showers are expected in the central mountains until around sunrise. Travel in these areas may be impacted by snow and icy roads mainly at pass level. Lingering moisture and clearing skies could result in pockets of fog into Thursday morning. Otherwise conditions become relatively dry. A quick moving shortwave skirts the region on Friday which could bring some increased clouds and a few light rain or snow showers over the higher terrain. The moisture is rather limited and the system is quick, so expect minor rain and snow amounts for now. A broad ridge of high pressure moves in late this week into the coming weekend, with temperatures warming to above seasonable levels and providing a much needed break from the recent wet weather.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Saturday - Wednesday: For the rest of the long term period, quiet weather makes a return to south central and southeastern Colorado. Overall, ridging will build across the region, bringing increased descent and drier air.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Early morning showers dry out by late morning today, with dry conditions thereafter.
- Warmer and drier conditions return for the first part of next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Today - Tonight: Active weather is expected early for Thursday, with quiet weather then prevailing for much of the day. A compact wave will be pushing/exiting to the southeast early in the day. While this feature will be pushing out through the morning, forcing associated with it will help support scattered rain showers across the plains early in the day. With that said, these showers will dissipate generally from northwest to southeast through the morning hours, with dry conditions expected by late morning. Behind this wave, shortwave ridging and increased subsidence is expected to develop. With this in place, dry conditions will then prevail through the rest of today and through tonight. Outside of all of that, partly to mostly cloudy skies early will give way to mostly clear skies during the afternoon hours, with winds remaining relatively light, around 10-15 mph. As for temperatures, a cool day is anticipated, with near to slightly below temperatures. For highs, the plains will be in the 50s, the valleys in the upper 40s to 50s, and the mountains in the low 30s to mid 40s. For lows, the plains will be the in the 30s, the valleys in the 20s, and the mountains in the upper 10s to 20s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Friday: For the end of the week, another brief period of active weather is expected for south central and southeastern Colorado. A broad and open wave will again push southeastward over the region through Friday. While forcing won't be overly strong with this wave, support from it, and a slight uptick in orographics, will help to support isolated to scattered shower develop along the mountains through the day. Snow levels will hover around 8,700ft, with snow above this and mostly rain below it. Any snow that falls along the higher terrain will be fairly minimal, around 1-1.5 inches or less. With that all said, any showers present are expected to dissipate overnight Friday as the wave weakens and pushes further to southeast. Beyond all of that, skies will be partly to mostly cloudy through much of the day, with mostly clear skies returning by Saturday morning. Temperatures for Friday will warm just a tad, with much of the area hovering around near seasonal values.

Saturday - Wednesday: For the rest of the long term period, quiet weather makes a return to south central and southeastern Colorado. Overall, ridging will build across the region, bringing increased descent and drier air. With this pattern in place, dry conditions are anticipated for the region. While there are some hints of weak waves being embedded within the flow, confidence remains very low (10-20%) on any influence from these features at this time. Outside of that, mostly clear to partly cloudy skies with relatively light winds can be expected. Looking at temperatures, a warming trend is anticipated, with much of the area warming to above seasonal values.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Behind that weak wave, strong ridging off the Pacific coast will continue to build through at least early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions will prevail through early next week, with only a very low chance of precipitation from a grazing shortwave late Thursday into Friday.
- Temperatures will stay below seasonal normals through the first half of the week, with building high pressure bringing more mild conditions beginning Sunday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Weak ridging has moved into Utah and southwest Wyoming this evening as the storm system that moved through earlier currently spinning over Colorado. With the influence of that storm system, temperatures have stayed on the cool side, with maxes averaging 5-10F below seasonal normals.

High clouds will be on the increase tomorrow as weak shortwave energy from the southern branch of a splitting Pacific Northwest storm system tracks across the area through early Friday. Guidance is overall trending even weaker with this feature, with any potential for showers with this wave quickly dwindling. Its presence will act to limit warming over the area, however, with persistence being the name of the game through Friday.

Behind that weak wave, strong ridging off the Pacific coast will continue to build through at least early next week. This will bring a steady warming trend over the weekend, resulting in temperatures up to 5F above seasonal normals by Sunday, with the potential for mild temperatures to continue for much of the upcoming week. Compared to yesterday, guidance seems to be trending toward solutions that favor the persistence of that blocking ridge for much of the upcoming week. A minority of solutions, however, including several GFS members, break down the ridge by midweek, allowing for a more active pattern to develop once again. Therefore, confidence in the forecast as day seven approaches remains low.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You could trigger an avalanche in wind-drifted snow above treeline that could be large enough to bury you.

The most dangerous slopes are where recent winds drifted snow into thicker, stiffer slabs on steep slopes above 12,000 feet. Look for and avoid wind-buffed snow surfaces and pillowy drifts in cross-loaded couloirs, rocky windward slopes, and lee slopes directly below ridgelines.
Safer travel options exist in wind-sheltered areas at lower elevations.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. Steer around steep slopes near ridgelines with continuous, firm snow cover. You might find these slopes at high elevations.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')

2755.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Fresh snow means you could trigger avalanches above treeline. Look for and avoid spots where winds drift the new snow. Those spots will be just below ridgelines, along gully walls, or around terrain features like rock outcrops. Because wind speeds with this storm are light, the drifted snow may be softer and less obvious than the typical Colorado wind slab. Most slopes near and below treeline lack enough snow to produce an avalanche.
